concepts.name: From Application to Instruction Execution
facts: A computation like Y = Model(X) descends from an application goal through algorithm, program, system software, OS scheduling, and hardware instruction execution before returning result Y.

The workflow begins by designing an algorithm Model with input data X, which a program expresses; system software then turns the program into an executable, parallel, and robust task, and the OS schedules and deploys tasks onto hardware. Hardware executes instructions and moves data to produce results, completing the computation and returning Y to the application.
Step 1: design an algorithm Model to solve a problem with input data X.
Step 2: a program expresses the algorithm.
Step 3: system software turns the program into an executable, parallel, and robust task.
Step 4: the OS schedules computing tasks and deploys them onto hardware; hardware executes instructions and moves data.
Step 5: computation completes and result Y is returned to the application.

concepts.name: Abstraction Layers in System Design
facts: Computing is organized as a transformation hierarchy in which each abstraction layer refines, expresses, translates, organizes or deploys the work of the layer above it, from the application problem down to digital logic.

The application/problem layer states the goal of the computation (AI inference, training, web search, recommendation); the algorithm layer supplies the method, dependency and parallelism (GEMM, attention, optimization, sampling); programs, languages and compilers give machine-facing expression (Python, C++, CUDA, Go); system software organizes executable work; the operating system provides process, thread, memory, scheduling and I/O; microarchitecture provides core, cache, RAM, pipeline, bus and controller; and digital logic provides gates, registers, wires and arithmetic units.
Application/problem = goal of the computation
Algorithm = method, dependency, parallelism
Program/Language/Compiler = machine-facing expression
System software organizes executable work; OS handles process, thread, memory, scheduling, I/O
Microarchitecture (core, cache, RAM, pipeline, bus, controller) and digital logic (gates, registers, wires, arithmetic units) are the lowest layers

concepts.name: CPU Core Architecture and Instruction Execution
facts: A computing core has an ALU for computing, a register file for data load/store, and instruction memory for pipelining, executing load, compute, and store steps.

Instruction execution is the last step of computing: load from RAM to register file, compute (add, mul) among registers, then store from register file to RAM. Execution steps: Load (RAM→register), Compute (register ops), Store (register→RAM)

concepts.name: Five-Stage Instruction Pipeline
facts: The five-stage pipeline (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB) overlaps data load/store time so that, ideally, one instruction completes per cycle after the pipeline fills.

Stages are Fetch (get instructions from instruction memory/cache), Decode (resolve opcode and operands), Execute (ALU, vector unit, load/store unit, tensor core), Memory Access (load/store through cache or memory hierarchy), and Write Back (update architectural state). For N instructions and M stages, total cycles = M + N – 1, giving average throughput N/(M+N−1) instructions per cycle and frequency × N/(M+N−1) instructions per second.
Goal: overlap time of data load/store
Perfect pipeline: one instruction completes per cycle after filling, no bubbles
Total Cycles = M + N – 1 for N instructions and M stages
Throughput per second = Frequency * N / (M + N - 1)
\(\text{Total Cycles} = M + N - 1\)

concepts.name: Pipeline Hazards
facts: A hazard is any condition that stalls the pipeline, producing bubbles and degraded efficiency; hazards come in data, control, and structural types.

Data hazards arise from data dependencies, listed as read-after-write (RAW), write-after-write (WAW), and write-after-read (WAR). Control hazards arise from branches: a deeper pipeline causes a worse penalty, and branches create uncertainty.

concepts.name: Data Forwarding and Register Renaming
facts: Data forwarding passes results directly to the consumer so it can execute earlier, while register renaming uses more registers to decouple dependencies.

Forwarding enables register-to-register or register-to-ALU paths, e.g., a result passed directly from a pipeline register to an ALU input, giving fewer stalls and higher pipeline efficiency. Register renaming uses more registers to decouple dependencies.
Forwarding enables register-to-register or register-to-ALU forwarding.

concepts.name: Out-of-Order and Superscalar Execution
facts: Out-of-order execution separates program, execution, and commit order, while superscalar cores try to execute multiple instructions every cycle through a wide pipeline.

OoO separates program order (written by the programmer), execution order (chosen by hardware), and commit order (updates architectural state); typically the compiler finds independent instruction sets to enable OoO and reduce stall time. Superscalar needs wide fetch, decode, multiple execution units, multiple load/store paths, wide writeback, and a multi-ported register file.
Program order, execution order, and commit order are separated.
The compiler typically finds independent instruction sets to enable OoO.
Superscalar tries to execute multiple instructions every cycle.
A wide pipeline needs wide fetch/decode/writeback, multiple execution units and load/store paths, and a multi-ported register file.
If the pipeline can issue N instructions concurrently, the CPU must resolve the resulting challenges.

concepts.name: Speculative Execution and Branch Prediction
facts: Speculative execution predicts next instructions and issues risky instructions for potentially large benefits, at the cost of wasted wrong-path work and recovery penalties.

Benefits are quick completion (low latency) and keeping the deep pipeline busy (high throughput). Costs are that wrong-path work wastes energy and cycles, and the recovery penalty grows with pipeline depth and speculation window. Branch prediction includes naïve static prediction, where the compiler finds branches that would not be taken and removes corresponding instructions to avoid control hazards, and dynamic branch prediction, which learns branch behavior automatically.
Prediction issues risky instructions on the chance of considerable benefits.
Benefit: quick completion (low latency) and a busy deep pipeline (high throughput).
Cost: wrong-path work wastes energy and cycles.
Recovery penalty grows with pipeline depth and speculation window.
Static prediction relies on the compiler; dynamic prediction learns branch behavior automatically.

concepts.name: Hyper-Threading and CPU Design Tradeoffs
facts: Hyper-threading introduces simultaneous multithreading so multiple hardware threads share one physical core, filling idle slots caused by cache misses, mispredictions, and dependency chains.

Even OoO superscalar cores have idle slot issues due to cache miss, branch misprediction, and dependency chains; SMT lets multiple hardware threads share one physical core, each logical thread having its own architectural state while execution units and caches are shared. The summary notes a modern CPU core spends many transistors on data forwarding, register renaming, and OoO execution, with ideal scenarios being control-heavy programs, irregular data structures, and OS and runtime services.

Idle slots come from cache miss, branch misprediction, and dependency chains.
SMT: multiple hardware threads share one physical core.

concepts.name: Control vs. Compute: Divergent Scaling Goals
facts: CPUs stay general for complex tasks and scale to hundreds of heavy cores, while GPUs target easily parallel tasks and scale to thousands of light cores for 10x–100x more computing power.

CPU hazards occur easily, forcing heavy microarchitectural optimization, and control logic such as branches and dependencies incurs synchronization among cores. GPU control logic is less and data parallelism is easy (e.g., vector processing), so GPUs scale to 1,000s–10,000s of light cores; the CPU is a few out-of-order, superscalar, hyper-threading heavy cores, the GPU many in-order, SIMD-pipeline light cores.
CPU goal: be general to complex tasks; hazards force many optimizations
GPU goal: be specific to easily parallel tasks with little control logic
CPU scales to hundreds of heavy cores; GPU to 1,000s–10,000s of light cores
GPU delivers 10x to 100x the computing power of CPU

concepts.name: Control Divergence and SIMD Utilization
facts: Branch divergence occurs when threads in a warp take different paths, so only a subset executes and SIMD pipeline utilization is wasted.

A GPU uses a SIMD pipeline to save area on control logic and groups scalar threads into warps; when threads inside warps branch to different execution paths, only a subset of threads execute. Divergence-free programming increases SIMD utilization, and in vector reduction the optimized program keeps all active threads in the same warp.

Result: only a subset of threads execute, wasting SIMD pipeline utilization.

concepts.name: Why AI Moved Toward GPU-Centric Computing
facts: Scaling laws made compute the bottleneck and Transformers made computation massively data-parallel, so the hardware target shifted to high-throughput training rather than low-latency single-thread execution.

Empirical loss improves predictably as compute, parameters, and data increase, and model size scales together with token count. Transformers expose SIMD/SIMT-friendly work because the most expensive layers are dense tensor kernels with parallel axes of batch, token, head, and hidden dimension.
Scaling laws turn AI into sustained FLOP demand, making compute the bottleneck.
The hardware target becomes high-throughput training, not low-latency single-thread execution.
Most expensive layers are dense tensor kernels: QKV projection, QK^T attention scores, AV product, FFN GEMM.
Parallel axes are batch, token, head, and hidden dimension; control flow is small and arithmetic intensity is high when tiled well.
CPU remains the host controller; the GPU becomes the dominant floating-point compute engine.

concepts.name: Race Conditions, Critical Sections, and Mutexes
facts: A race condition occurs when multiple threads access a shared resource and the final result depends on timing; a critical section is code that only one thread may execute at a time.

In the example sum += local_sum, each thread loads sum, adds local_sum and stores sum; if two threads run concurrently, both may read the old value and one write overwrites the other. A mutex serializes access to the critical section, avoiding races on protected shared state at the cost of lock contention.
